CORRECTION, AND IT IS THE FINDING OF THE DAY: the watchdog was NEUTERED by the m53456 "BEB-2360 SUBTRACTION" — the kick ladder deleted on the theory that an always-on dispatcher restarts a lapsed lease. That theory fails in the only case that matters, when the DISPATCHER is the wedged party. So 46 stalls with zero recoveries was not a broken watchdog, it was a watchdog with its hands removed on purpose. Restoring out-of-band actuation is right, and it is BEB-2360 landed into what exists rather than a third thing — correct per 65265.

CAUTION on the kick ladder: judge by last_pass.at and tick_n MOVING, never by a 200 — you already have this and it is the single most important line in your plan. A kick that returns 200 and changes nothing is the same lie as a deploy that reports done. Cooldown 120s is fine. Escalate loud after 3 non-taking kicks.

ADDED, and I want it in the same pass: the watchdog is now the OUT-OF-BAND WITNESS from 65260. So it must treat UNREACHABLE and EMPTY as red, not as quiet. Today get_state returned reds EMPTY while the dispatcher was unreachable and the board read all-clear. A witness that goes silent when its subject dies is not a witness. Detection budget 10s, not 60.

NOTED AND ACCEPTED: watchdog holds no deploy credential and a hard wedge needs a redeploy it cannot perform. Do not paper over that — when the ladder exhausts, the RED must name that the remaining action requires a credential the watchdog does not hold. That is a real boundary and it should be visible rather than silently retried.

FABLE — PERMISSIONS UP FRONT, AND THE BETTER ANSWER UNDERNEATH. Adds to BEB-5527 item 1a (BEB-3853 NO PROMPT).

ALEX'S COMPLAINT, and it is a real cost: he sits with a session for an hour only to approve an edit 55 minutes in. He has told CC to think ahead and it keeps not happening. His time is spent waiting to press a button.

IMMEDIATE FIX — DECLARE THE WHOLE PERMISSION SET AT THE START:
Before a work block begins, CC enumerates EVERY permission the planned edits will need — every path, every worker, every store — and requests them ONCE, up front, as a single set. Not one prompt per file, 55 minutes in. If the set turns out to be incomplete mid-run, that is a planning failure to record, not a reason to interrupt Alex again.
THE GRAPH HELPS HERE, use it: the service graph already knows which files, workers and stores a ticket's surface touches. Derive the permission set from the graph rather than discovering it one refusal at a time. That is what "think ahead" looks like mechanically instead of as an instruction CC keeps failing.

BUT THE REAL ANSWER IS ALEX'S SECOND POINT, and it outranks the first: MOVE IT TO SETTINGS INSTEAD OF AN EDIT.
Most of what CC asks permission for is a VALUE, not a structure. A value change should never be an edit at all — it is a settings-row write, which needs no file permission and no approval, and takes seconds. That is BEB-3851 SETTINGS FIRST, and this is now its strongest argument: every value that lives in a row is one fewer permission prompt, forever.
Alex's example, taken literally: "services like MCP change a setting instead of an edit." So a service that today needs a code change to alter behaviour gets its behaviour on rows and an MCP tool to write them. Then CC changes it by calling a tool, with no file access, no prompt, no deploy.

THE ORDER THIS IMPLIES:
1. Can it be a settings row? Write the row. No permission needed. This is the normal path and it should become most of them.
2. No row exists yet? The code change's deli

FABLE — REUSABLE INFRA IS THE GOAL, AND REUSABILITY IS GRAPHED. Standing rule, Alex 2026-08-25. Add to BEB-5527 as a condition on every item, not a new item.

ALEX'S POINT: the goal is DURABLE, REUSABLE INFRA — not a pile of one-offs that each get built, forgotten and rebuilt. If a thing is reusable infra, say so, fill it out properly, and GRAPH THE REUSABILITY so it is not forgotten or lost. That is how the estate stops re-deriving what it already has.

THE RULE, applied to everything on 5527 and after:
1) NAME IT AS INFRA OR NOT. Every piece landed says plainly: reusable infra, or one-off for this ticket. No silent middle. If it is infra, it gets the full treatment now rather than a thinner version to be redone later.
2) REGISTER IT AS A GRAPH NODE at landing (BEB-2071/2484 — nodes, never a new registry). The node carries what it is FOR, its interface, its source path, its spec doc, its contract verdict, and its USAGE COUNT.
3) GRAPH THE REUSE ITSELF. Every consumer is an EDGE to that node. So "has anyone built X" returns what it was for, whether it was proven, and who already uses it. A node with zero consumer edges is BUILT/UNWIRED — visible, not silently orphaned.
4) CHECK THE GRAPH BEFORE BUILDING. If a node already answers the need, use it. Building a second one when a node exists is the defect this rule prevents — today's example: the bespoke metrics worker you correctly retired in favour of ABCMS blocks.
5) LOSE NOTHING. The reason for the node and its reusability travel WITH it. An infra piece whose purpose is not on the node gets rebuilt by whoever comes next, which is the cost we keep paying.

THIS IS ALREADY THE PATTERN IN THREE PLACES — do not build a fourth mechanism, extend these: BEB-3507 block library (blocks as registered graph nodes, reusable across dashes), BEB-3908 APP ROADMAP GRAPH (app nodes with derived scores and traceable evidence), BEB-2071 registries-become-graphs. Same node shape, same edges.

Alex flagged Vercel's Run SDK, published TODAY (2026-08-25): https://vercel.com/blog/introducing-run

What it is: a package for executing untrusted JS/TS in a fresh QuickJS context inside a worker thread, with no direct route to Node or the network. The application exposes narrow HOST FUNCTIONS that become callable globals in the sandbox; credentials stay in the application. It is the runtime powering code mode in the AI SDK.

Three things in it are directly ours:

1) HOST FUNCTIONS ARE THE PERMISSION MODEL WE SPECCED TODAY. Their guidance: host functions should map to product actions (orders.refund(id)) rather than a generic request function, because that gives the application one clear place to check the caller. That is exactly 65296 — narrow named operations instead of file access, and settings rows instead of edits.

2) INTERRUPT / RESUME IS THE APPROVAL PROBLEM SOLVED PROPERLY. A host function can interrupt for approval or auth; the result carries a signed token, and on resume the program REPLAYS with settled host calls using their RECORDED RESULTS — completed work does not run again. Note what that is: replay with recorded inputs, which is 65265's replayability requirem

THE DIG — Vercel's eve (open source, Apache-2.0, npm `eve`, github.com/vercel/eve, launched 2026-06-17; they run 100+ agents on it). The comparison is against OUR thrash, and today gave us the numbers to compare with: 560 identical deploys, 4,823 identical comments, one question asked ~50 times, 46 stalls with zero recoveries.

Their shape, per their docs and coverage:
- AN AGENT IS A DIRECTORY OF FILES. Instructions, skills, tools, auth, channels, schedule. The directory is the contract — the tree shows what the agent is, what it does, where it lives, and when it acts on its own. Compare ours: an agent's behaviour is spread across prompt text, ticket descriptions, machinery code and bridge prose, with no single legible definition anywhere.
- DURABLE EXECUTION AS THE DEFAULT UNIT. Every conversation is a workflow with each step CHECKPOINTED; a session pauses, survives a crash OR A DEPLOY, and resumes at the last completed step. Built on their open Workflow SDK. Ours re-derives from the ticket text every pass — the root cause under every bad number today.
- APPROVALS THAT DO NOT BURN. Any action can require approval; the agent pauses indefinitely WITHOUT CONSUMING COMPUTE, then continues from where it stopped. That is Alex's minute-55 problem without the burn, and it composes with 3853 rather than fighting it.
- SANDBOXED COMPUTE. Agent-generated code is untrusted by default, own sandbox per agent, separate security context from the harness controlling it. Sandbox backend is an ADAPTER — swappable.
- CONNECTIONS ARE FILES pointing at an MCP server or an OpenAPI API. Declared, not hunted. Same instinct as BEB-2192's declare-by-name and today's 65225.
- TRACING AND EVALS built in — every run produces a trace, plus a tool

FABLE — NOT DROPPED: CHAIN SPEED, and Kitesurf. Alex raised this yesterday and it has not moved. Tomorrow, alongside the eve dig (65312), not tonight.

THE ASK, in Alex's terms: optimise the SPEED OF THE CHAIN from Orky input to change live — total, boot to shipped — using Playwright. And Kitesurf may load faster, or be easier, than what we run now.

WHY IT MATTERS AND WHY IT KEEPS SLIPPING: today's headline numbers were about the loop not landing at all, so nobody looked at how LONG a landing takes. Both matter. A loop that claims 20 slots but takes an hour per pass is still a slow loop. And chain latency is the thing Alex feels — he asks for something and waits.

WHAT I WANT MEASURED, END TO END, NOT PER-STAGE GUESSES:
1. TOTAL WALL TIME, Orky input → change live and verified. One number, then the breakdown. Today's tick times were 40-125s just for the dispatcher pass, which is a fraction of the real chain.
2. WHERE IT GOES: propose · refine · claim · codegen · deploy · contract_run · recording. Which stage owns the most seconds. Name the top three by real measurement.
3. BROWSER TIME SPECIFICALLY. Playwright drives screenshot_url, record_url and contract_run — every ticket ends in a browser now, and per the standing rule every ticket also produces a RECORDING. That makes browser startup and page-load a per-ticket tax, paid thousands of times. Cold browser boot, page load, assertion pass, recording write — measure each.
4. KITESURF: evaluate it against our current browser path on the two things Alex named — LOAD SPEED and EASE. Honest comparison, real numbers, including whether it runs where we need it to. If it is not faster or not easier, say so plainly and we drop it.

CONSTRAINTS:
- Measure before changing anything. This is a profiling job first; the fix follows the numbers.
- Replay applies (65265): capture the run so a change can be re-run against the same chain and the delta forecast rather than guessed.
- Reuse rule applies (65304): whatever the browser ha

FABLE — ADDENDUM TO 65314. WebGL is a hard requirement on the browser harness. Alex: "not sure Kitesurf loads WebGL, but sure, try it."

He is right to flag it and it is the disqualifier, so test it FIRST rather than last.

WHY IT MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY: the 3JS loop viz (BEB-2909) is now the standard per-ticket deliverable — every ticket produces an animated workflow recording, and that recording is three.js. If a browser harness cannot render WebGL, it cannot record the viz, and the proof-debt work (BEB-2488/3603) dies with it. A faster browser that cannot see our own visuals is useless to us.

TEST ORDER FOR KITESURF — first failure ends the evaluation, no further work:
1. WEBGL RENDERS AT ALL. Point it at https://abilifi-viz.alex-rollin.workers.dev and confirm the scene actually paints — not a 200, not a title, PIXELS. Fable verified that page tonight at 390px with real state on the current harness, so there is a known-good baseline to compare against.
2. WEBGL RECORDS. Not just renders — record_url must capture the animation, with motion visible across frames. A still frame of a moving scene is a fail.
3. Only if 1 and 2 pass: measure load speed and ease against the current path per 65314.

VERDICT LINE, whichever way it goes: "Kitesurf renders/records WebGL: yes/no" with the evidence, then the speed numbers if it got that far. If it fails on WebGL, say so in one line and we keep what we have — that is a complete and useful answer, not a failed task.

Note for the wider profiling: whatever we run must render WebGL, load fast, and record. Those are the three, in that order of necessity. Do not optimise the first two at the cost of the third.
